reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: A collection of pus in the spinal epidural space that is a neurosurgical emergency because of the risk of irreversible cord compression
The classic triad of back pain, fever, and neurological deficit is present in only a minority, so a high index of suspicion is essential
Symptoms often progress through localised back pain, then radicular pain, then motor or sensory deficit and sphincter dysfunction, and finally paralysis
Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, and infection may spread haematogenously or contiguously from vertebral osteomyelitis or paraspinal infection
Risk factors include injecting drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression, indwelling catheters, spinal instrumentation, and recent epidural procedures
Urgent MRI with contrast is the investigation of choice and should not be delayed once the diagnosis is considered

Management principles combine emergency surgical decompression and drainage for neurological compromise with prolonged targeted antibiotics; selected stable patients without deficit may be managed medically with close monitoring
Once a significant neurological deficit is established, the window for functional recovery is short, making speed of intervention critical
reference.pathophysiology: A spinal epidural abscess forms when bacteria reach the epidural space by haematogenous seeding, contiguous spread from vertebral osteomyelitis or a paraspinal focus, or direct inoculation during a spinal procedure. Accumulating pus causes neurological injury through two mechanisms: direct mechanical compression of the spinal cord or cauda equina and vascular compromise, with septic thrombophlebitis and arterial disruption producing cord ischaemia and infarction. This combination explains why deficits can progress rapidly and become irreversible if decompression is delayed.
additionalDifferentials: Vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis without abscess
Acute disc herniation with cord compression
Guillain-Barre syndrome in the setting of ascending weakness
infectionMimics: Metastatic epidural cord compression from malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Urgent MRI of the whole spine with contrast to localise the abscess and assess cord compression
Culture of aspirated or surgically drained pus to guide antibiotics
Screening for a primary source such as endocarditis or vertebral osteomyelitis
Assessment for skip lesions, since abscesses may involve multiple non-contiguous levels
redFlags: Any new or progressing motor weakness, sensory level, or bladder or bowel dysfunction indicating cord or cauda equina compression requiring emergency decompression
Rapid neurological deterioration signalling a closing window for recovery
Back pain with fever in an injecting drug user or immunocompromised patient
reference.prognosis: Outcome hinges on neurological status at the time of intervention; patients treated before a major deficit develops usually do well, whereas established paralysis, especially if present for more than a day or two before decompression, often does not recover fully.
pitfalls: Waiting for the full triad of back pain, fever, and deficit before considering the diagnosis
Delaying MRI or surgical referral once suspicion is raised
Failing to image the entire spine and missing non-contiguous abscesses
Underestimating how quickly a mild deficit can progress to permanent paralysis
management: Arrange emergency surgical decompression and drainage of pus (laminectomy and evacuation) when there is neurological deficit or cord compression, as timely intervention determines recovery

Give prolonged intravenous antibiotics, empirically covering Staphylococcus aureus including meticillin-resistant strains (vancomycin) plus Gram-negative organisms, then narrowed to culture-directed therapy
Obtain urgent whole-spine MRI with contrast and immediate neurosurgical referral, with serial neurological observations to detect deterioration
Achieve source control by treating vertebral osteomyelitis or endocarditis and removing infected indwelling catheters or spinal hardware
Provide supportive care with analgesia, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and bladder and bowel management
Escalate immediately for any progressive motor, sensory or sphincter deterioration, and arrange rehabilitation and physiotherapy for residual deficits
